# Keep the Active Work Item Accurate

The work tracker is the source of truth for current work.

- Before substantial work, use the `work-on` skill. Read the active item's requirements, state, next step, and blockers.
- Save the owner's decisions, requirements, and corrections in the item or its linked document before moving on.
- When the work needs the owner's decision, add it to the item's Open Questions with "Decision needed from: owner" and set the item's `waiting_on` to `owner`. The `work-decide` skill records the answer.
- `build` and `data-load` work needs approved requirements before it starts. A later stage does not revoke that approval.
- After the owner accepts agent-led delivery, ask how the team is arranged. That choice authorizes helpers for that goal only.
- Mark an item Done only after the owner approves the result.
- Before ending unfinished work, record the exact next step in the item.

`toolkit work lifecycle` prints the stages, statuses, and approval gates. "Where information goes" in `AGENTS.md` is the routing table; the `work-delegate` skill holds the delivery offer and team questions, and the `handoff` skill holds the handoff steps.

# Humanize Anything Sent to Another Person

Any text that will leave the project and be read by someone other than the owner
is run through the `humanizer` skill before the owner sees the final version.
Use the `unslop` skill when `humanizer` is not installed. That covers emails,
chat messages, support case text and comments, GitHub issues, pull request
descriptions, client documents, and any file made to hand to someone else.

Keep every fact, name, id, number, and date exactly as it was. Write it in the
owner's voice, first person, when it goes out under their name.

It does not apply to chat replies to the owner, work items, project knowledge,
code, or commit messages.

# Review and Save Project Memory

This rule applies to the main agent. The project memory system is chosen at setup and recorded in `.toolkit.json`; with built-in memory it is the local `.memory/` folder. It is the single project memory store. Claude's native auto-memory and the `claude-toolkit` Second Brain plugin are disabled for this project. The session-start briefing shows the current focus in Claude Code and Codex. Do not treat a hook reminder as a save decision.

## Decide the destination first

Read the memory criteria (`.memory/memory-criteria.md` with built-in memory) and the likely owning record. Send current focuses, owner to-dos, and handoff context to the current focus; sourced terminology to the glossary; qualifying otherwise-unowned durable context to a topic; active work to the chosen tracker; decisions for the whole project to `DECISIONS.md`; accepted delivered behavior to requirements; the technical approach to the design kept with its work item; verified current structure to the System Guide; and repeatable procedure to instructions or a skill. Raw external documentation stays in its source folder. A small memory pointer can route future sessions to a hard-to-find authority without copying its body.

Review on explicit remember/forget requests, corrections, standing preferences, meaningful decisions or discoveries, significant fixes or episodes, people/tool/reference changes, focus shifts, work-item completion, and handoffs. The toolkit's `UserPromptSubmit` hook flags only explicit keep phrases, and its Stop hook checks once per turn that such a phrase was handled. Do not save on every hook reminder or every turn. A review can end with no memory.

## Approval

The `memory-save` skill holds the approval policy: what the owner's own words authorize, what needs a yes in onboarding mode, what trusted mode allows, and what always needs the owner. The mode is `memory.approval` in `.toolkit.json`; only an explicit owner instruction changes it. A yes authorizes the shown operation and meaning only. Silence does not. An unanswered save question is kept as a proposal: the agent does not rely on it, and `work-decide` shows it to the owner until he approves or rejects it. The `memory-save` skill says how.

If the owner says a proposed item should not be memory, withdraw it. Save only a general selection rule, as a `feedback` memory, if their feedback supplies one; do not restate the rejected fact in the current focus or another topic. Review similar candidates against that rule from then on.

## Saving and completion

The main agent saves memory itself through the `memory-save` skill, which runs `toolkit memory` commands; there is no curator agent. Search first with `toolkit memory find`, then save with `toolkit memory save`, retire with `toolkit memory retire`, and write the current focus or glossary with `toolkit memory focus --set-file` or `toolkit memory glossary --set-file`. The commands lock memory, refuse stale edits, and rebuild the index.

For a focus-only change or already-authorized glossary maintenance, save without a lasting-memory question. Several independent signals can be grouped into one save; do not run parallel writes against the same topic or index. Before claiming a save succeeded, read it back with `toolkit memory get` and run `toolkit doctor`; tell the user briefly what was retained or what needs a decision.

# Write Artifacts in Plain English

An artifact is something an agent generates for a person to look at: a
diagram, a chart, a dashboard, a visualization, a mockup, a slide deck, a
published page, or a generated document. This rule is about the words inside
one: the title, the headings, the labels, the notes, the captions, the body
text.

The project's output style says how the agent talks in chat. The words inside
an artifact follow the same style. This rule exists because the output style
reaches only the main chat: a helper agent, a skill, or a Codex session that
makes an artifact never sees it. Read the active style file when there is
one. Where this rule and that file differ, the style file wins.

## Write about the subject

Every word describes the thing the artifact shows. The reader opened it to
learn about that thing, not about the artifact or the conversation that
produced it.

- Do not narrate the artifact. "Here is where the change lands, but only the
  key pieces" says nothing about the system. Cut it, or say what changed.
- Do not tell the reader what matters. "Here is the load-bearing decision"
  tells them how to feel. Write the decision.
- Bring in the conversation only when it is the fact. A quote earns its place
  when the exact words are what the reader needs, and then it says who said
  it and when. A quote the reader cannot place is noise.

## A heading names what is under it

A heading is a label, not a hook. It says what the reader is about to look
at, in the words of the subject.

The four headings below are an example: a page of options for who can see and
edit which projects in a team web app. The left column sells the section; the
right column names it.

| Written | Say instead |
|---|---|
| Three ways to build the team tree, pick one | Team structure options |
| One question decides the whole shape | Decision: can a team lead edit their own team's projects? |
| Four facts that rule out the most obvious answers | How team access works |
| What shape actually hands to a real person | Project visibility by role |

A number belongs in a heading when the number is the fact: "Three departments
share one role". "Three ways to build it" only counts the section below, and
the reader can count.

## Use the real name

Call a thing what the system calls it, every time. In that example the real
names are team structure, project visibility, sharing rule, admin access, and
permission group. The page used picture words instead: "shape" for the team
structure, "lever" for a setting, "leaks" for access people should not have,
"flows up" for a manager getting access to their team's projects. That is
figurative language, and it is not allowed. It makes the reader translate, and
a reader who does not know the system cannot.

A term the reader may not know gets a plain definition the first time it
appears. After that, the term is used unchanged.

A box or label carries the real name. Anything it needs to say about itself
is one plain line.

## Say the plain thing

Use the active output style inside the artifact. This artifact rule also requires:

- Common words. Short sentences. One idea each.
- No figurative or metaphorical language. No idioms, no jokes, no picture word
  standing in for a real thing.
- No preamble. Start with the content.
- No closing line that sums up or cheers.
- Fewer words, never fewer facts. Every number, name, date, and quotation
  stays exactly as it is.

## What this rule does not decide

How the artifact is laid out: how many boxes, what an arrow says, where a
note goes, whether there is a key. Every artifact is different, and the agent
making it decides. This rule decides the words.

# Work requirements

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Interviews the owner and writes what the result must do, never how to build it; every answer lands in the work item. Track these steps with the host's plan tool (Claude Code: the task list; Codex: `update_plan`), not in the reply.

## Steps

1. Find the item as `work-on` does; none exists, create it with his words as the Starting request. Requirements already approved and no change asked: open the skill the item's "Continue with" names and stop.
   `toolkit work show <id>`
   `toolkit work new --title '<title>' --type <type> --stage 01-discovery`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Starting request' --text '<his exact words>'`
2. Move it to refinement once requirements are being written. Before the first question, read the item and what the project already knows (`references/interview.md`, section 2).
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 02-refinement`
   `toolkit memory find '<topic>'`
3. Restate the goal in one sentence ("So the goal is X?"). Write the Agreed goal after a yes, and always before asking for approval.
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Agreed goal' --text '<goal>'`
4. Ask one question at a time, most basic first, each with a recommended answer and a short reason (`references/interview.md`, sections 3 and 4).
5. Save each answer before the next question: `R-xx` blocks and the Acceptance list in the format in `references/requirement-format.md`; anything unanswered as an Open Questions row, with the item waiting on the owner while one of his is open.
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Active requirements' --set-file <file>`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Open Questions' --append-row '| <next Q-id> | <question> | R-02 | Open | owner |'`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on owner`
6. A change to an approved requirement: edit the `R-xx`, keep the old wording in its Decision record, set it back to Refining, move the item to refinement, and say what the change affects when the item is past stage 03 (`references/interview.md`, section 7). The earlier approval stays on the record, and the stage command says so: it covered the requirements as they were, so ask him to approve the changed ones (step 8) before anything is built on them.
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 02-refinement`
7. Spec check, before asking for approval and whenever the owner says "check the spec": brief the `requirements-analyst` and handle its findings (`references/spec-check.md`).
8. Ask for approval and record his yes with the requirements checklist in `references/approvals.md`, section 2. Then a `build` or `data-load` item goes to `solution-design`, unless he agreed to skip the design.
   `toolkit work approve <id> --requirements --by <owner>`
9. Lead with "Not saved" on a failed write. Validate, update the current focus when the next step changed (`references/current-focus.md`), and hand back to `work-on` unless the owner stops. End with the one question or the exact words that continue.
   `toolkit work validate <id>`

## Gotchas

- Run each `toolkit` command alone: never joined by `&&`, `;`, or a pipe, and never from a script (in Codex that runs it inside the sandbox, where it fails). One-line values go in single quotes, never double quotes; an apostrophe inside them is `'\''` in Claude Code and ’ (U+2019) in Codex, or reword the text. Section text goes on standard input (`--set-file -`) in Claude Code, and in `--text '<text>'` or a `mktemp -d` file in Codex (`references/toolkit-commands.md`, "Text in a command").
- Ask in the reply text, never through a question tool. "Grill me" or "ask me questions" means one question at a time, never a batch.
- Build ideas never go into requirements: they go under Notes > Solution options and considerations.
- The CLI refuses the approval while the Agreed goal still holds the template text.
- Local and Notion trackers: never write the Requirements "Overall status" line; the approve command sets it. GitHub Issues and Jira have no approve command, so there the agent writes it after his yes.
- A change to an approved `R-xx` sends the item back to refinement and needs approval again.
- The spec check changes nothing without the owner's yes.
- "Give me options first" is not a requirements approval: go to `solution-design` with the open choices kept visible.
- GitHub Issues or Jira: `toolkit work` exits with code 3. Edit the issue's Requirements section as `references/tracker-github.md` or `references/tracker-jira.md` says.

## Agents

- `requirements-analyst` (`references/agent-requirements-analyst.md`): the spec check in step 7. The brief is in `references/spec-check.md`.
- `researcher` (`references/agent-researcher.md`): one per fact the owner cannot answer (a platform limit, what the existing build does).
- Brief them as `references/helpers.md` says.

# Work Safely in a Shared Repository

Other sessions edit this repository now. Before your first edit, run:

```
git worktree list
git status
git fetch origin && git log --oneline -10
```

- No remote (`git remote` prints nothing): skip `git fetch`, and never report a fetch failure as a blocker.
- An unknown worktree, moved branch, or change you did not make means other sessions are live. Do not fix it. Tell the owner.
- Code, rules, skills, hooks, settings: use your own worktree and branch (`git worktree add .claude/worktrees/<name> -b claude/<name>`). Exception: a one-file edit asked for directly.
- Documentation-only saves: open the `publish-docs` skill.
- In the shared primary checkout, never switch branches, reset, rebase, or stash.
- Never touch another session's branch or uncommitted work.
- Stage paths by name. Never `git add -A`, `git add .`, or `git commit -a`. Read the full staged diff.
- Never hand-edit a generated file.
- Before taking a sequential number, check every tracker folder, worktree, and the remote. On a later collision, renumber only your own.
- Land implementation by pull request, merged with the owner's approval. A standing merge instruction the owner gave for this project counts.
- Before a merge, compare `git diff --name-only <default-branch>...<branch>` with `git status` in the primary checkout. A file in both: stop, name it, ask the owner.
- After the merge, remove your worktree and branch.

# Local Work-Item Folders

This project tracks work in local folders under `.work-items/`. The folder is
Git-ignored, lives in the main checkout, and is shared by every worktree. It is
not backed up by Git: `toolkit export` is the backup.

## An item is found by its ID, not its path

- An item is a folder holding a record, `WORK-ITEM.md`, and `DESIGN.md` when a
  design exists. The frontmatter `id` (for example `WI-001`) is the item's
  identity. The folder name and the file name may change.
- Refer to items by ID everywhere. Find an item's files with
  `toolkit work show <id> --path`. Never guess a path.
- Create items only with `toolkit work new`. It takes the next ID under a lock,
  so parallel sessions never pick the same one. IDs are never reused.

## The owner may move folders, and the agent adapts

- The owner may move, rename, nest, or group item folders by hand. That is
  normal. `toolkit work sync` finds every item again by its ID; the session
  hooks and every `toolkit work` command run it. Report what moved and continue.
  Use the `work-organize` skill to reconcile anything the sync reports as
  missing or duplicated.
- A record inside another item's folder is that item's sub-item: its `parent`
  follows its location. A plain folder with no record is a group and changes no
  parent.
- `archive/` is a reserved group. Items there are hidden from the briefing and
  from `toolkit work next`.
- Never move, group, archive, or rename items on your own initiative. When the
  owner asks, use `toolkit work move <id> --under <id|group|archive|root>`.

## What the tracker ignores, and what it generates

- Ignored: `work-item-template/`, any folder whose name starts with `_` or `.`,
  and any record whose title is still `<Work item title>`.
- Generated by `toolkit work sync`: `DASHBOARD.md`. State kept by `toolkit work`:
  `.toolkit-state.json` (the ID-to-path map and the highest ID used). Never edit
  either by hand.
- Change frontmatter fields (stage, status, parent, waiting on, approvals) only
  with `toolkit work` commands. Body sections may be edited directly or with
  `toolkit work edit`; the hook checks the record after each edit.
- Keep any other files the owner put in an item folder.

# Memory save

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Saves, corrects, or retires one fact in the project's memory with `toolkit memory` commands, or sends the fact to its proper home. It never edits memory files by hand. Memory keeps one record per concept (for example `feedback_ways_of_working`, `project_billing`), with one `##` section per fact; an `event_` record holds one episode.

## Steps

Track these steps in the host's plan tool (Claude Code: the task list; Codex: `update_plan`), not in the reply.

1. Decide the home with the memory criteria (`.memory/memory-criteria.md` with built-in memory, which wins; otherwise `references/memory-criteria.md`). Not memory: send it to its home ("Where other things go" below) and stop.
2. Find the concept it belongs in, and any section that already holds it. List the concepts of its type (title, summary, updated date), search, and read each likely concept whole, with its version. The save's duplicate check compares wording, so only this search finds a section the new fact contradicts (for example "Mondays" against "Tuesdays").
   `toolkit memory list --type <type>`
   `toolkit memory find '<topic>'`
   `toolkit memory get <key> --json`
3. Read the approval mode and apply "Approval policy" below. When it says ask, ask and wait.
   `toolkit config get memory.approval`
4. Pick where it goes ("Choosing the concept" below), write the section text in the record format (`references/record-format.md`), and save with the form for the case ("Save forms" below).
5. Exit code 2 saved nothing. Read the "Error:" line. "Belongs in the concept <key>": add it there with the command the "Fix:" line prints, or, when it is a different concept, save again with `--new-concept`. Records listed: the duplicate check. "Changed since it was read": read it again and redo the change. Any other rule: fix the text as the message says. `references/replacing-and-retiring.md`, section 2, has each case.
6. "Forget that" right after a section save: run the "Undo:" command the save printed (it removes that section). About a whole concept: retire it, with his words as the reason. Delete only when his own words say delete ("Approval policy").
   `toolkit memory retire <key> --reason '<his words>'`
7. An owner to-do with no work item, or a change to what is happening now: update the current focus (`references/current-focus.md`). A project term: update the glossary (`references/glossary.md`).
8. A preference a project setting can enforce (for example "I hate tabs" and `.editorconfig`): save it, then offer that change too.
9. Read the record back, check, and reply in one line ("Replies" below). End with the question still waiting for the owner, or the exact words that continue.
   `toolkit memory get <key>`
   `toolkit doctor`

## Approval policy

This is the only written copy of the memory approval policy.

- The owner's own words are the approval: "remember", "from now on", "always", "never", "forget", or a correction. Save now, with `--approved-by <owner>`. That includes a fact about a named person he asks you to remember ("remember that Priya's last day is October 15").
- `onboarding` mode (the default): something the agent inferred gets one yes-or-no line first, in exactly this form: "Save to memory: <one-line summary>?". Save after his yes (`references/proposals.md` when a proposal was saved for the question).
- A preference or fact he mentions in passing, without a keep phrase or an instruction ("screenshots were more useful than the text"), is inferred: ask "Save to memory: ...?" first. Only his keep words, or his yes to that question, are an approval.
- Recommend a yes only with evidence from this project (what he said, what happened, and when). With none, ask without a recommendation.
- `trusted` mode: a routine fact the agent is sure of is saved without asking and reported in one line, with no approver. The record says "Trusted grant".
- In either mode, always ask first for anything about a named person or personal details that he did not ask you to remember, for more than five records at once, and for a change to this policy.
- A delete needs his own words about that record ("delete it", "remove it for good"), or his yes to a numbered list that shows the delete. Do not ask again: the host asks him to confirm `toolkit memory delete`, and that prompt is the confirmation. "Forget that" is a retire, never a delete.
- A yes covers only the change and the meaning shown. Silence is never a yes.
- `--approved-by` is only for a change his words or his yes covered. Give his name exactly as the project settings hold it (`project.owner`, for example "Mike Rihm", not "Mike").
- A concept's `authorization` line is the approval of the concept. A section save never changes it; when the save's approval differs, the CLI records it on that section's Evidence and limits line (`references/record-format.md`, "Frontmatter").
- An unanswered "Save to memory?" stays a proposal until he answers (`references/proposals.md`). Never drop it, and never save it with an approver.
- Only the owner switches the mode, in his own words ("you can save routine things without asking me"). Save his words as a `feedback` record with the date, then run one of:
  `toolkit config set memory.approval trusted`
  `toolkit config set memory.approval onboarding`

## Choosing the concept

- One concept is one subject a future session would look up as a whole: how he wants the agent to work (`feedback_ways_of_working`), the billing setup (`project_billing`), his role and habits (`user_profile`), where dashboards live (`reference_dashboards`).
- The fact has the concept's type. Add it to the existing concept of that type whose title and summary cover it, as a new section. The heading names the sub-topic in a few words ("Force-push", "Refund window").
- The concept already has a heading for this sub-topic: add under it with `--append`. The fact corrects what a section says: replace that section with `--expect`.
- No concept of that type covers it: start a new one. Its slug and title name the concept, not the fact (`project_billing`, not `project_invoices_go_out_on_the_1st`), and its summary says what the whole concept covers.
- An event is always its own record: one episode per `event_` record.
- Two concepts fit: pick the one a future session would open first, and link the other from the section's **Related memories** line.

## Save forms

`<file>` is `-` in Claude Code, with the body on standard input after a quoted heredoc (`<<'EOF'`). In Codex give `--body '<text>'` in place of `--body-file <file>`. `references/record-format.md` shows both.

- A new concept, with its first fact:

- A question he has not answered yet: either form with `--proposal` in place of `--approved-by`. With `--concept`, `--description` is the fact in one line; the concept changes only after his yes.

- One more fact under a heading the concept already has: add `--append` to the first form.

- An event (its own record):

| The owner's words are about | Home | Open |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Project work, a task, a bug, "add it to the backlog" | A work item | `work-on` |
| A decision for the whole project | `DECISIONS.md` | `work-decide` |
| A requirement for a work item | The item's requirements | `work-requirements` |
| Behavior already delivered | `requirements/` | none |
| How a change is built | The item's design | `solution-design` |
| Verified current structure of the system | `system-guide/` | none |
| Outside documentation | `ai-external-knowledge/` | none |
| A standing rule for how agents work here | A rule-file change, proposed to him | none |
| His to-do with no work item and no time | Current focus, Untracked to-dos | step 7 |
| A to-do with a time ("at 9 tomorrow") | A scheduled reminder, outside memory | the host's scheduling tool |
| A project term | The glossary | step 7 |

- A proposal: "Saved as a proposal for your yes or no: <title>."

## Steps

1. Build the queue. The command lists each decision once: requirements waiting for approval, proposed designs, results at stage 11, Open Questions rows the owner decides, and memory proposals. Its "Agent to-do" lines are not decisions. A delivery offer belongs to `work-delegate`: open it after his other decisions.
   `toolkit work decisions`
2. He gave an answer without being asked ("approved", "go with B"): match it to exactly one waiting decision; when two could match, ask which, naming both. A bare "yes", "ok", or "looks good" with no question asked is not an answer (`references/approvals.md`, section 1).
3. Otherwise start with the count and one short line for every waiting decision, memory proposals included ("3 decisions wait on you: the WI-004 design, the WI-006 result, and a memory proposal about deploy days."). Then take them one at a time, the one blocking the most work first: what is decided, the choices, your recommendation and its main reason, and what happens after each answer. One decision per message, in the reply text.
4. An approval: read the item, then run that gate's checklist in `references/approvals.md` (requirements: section 2; design: section 3; result: section 4). A result with no independent acceptance check since its last build (the command prints a note): open `work-check` first, which runs it whoever built the change.
   `toolkit work show <id>`
5. An Open Questions answer: save his words first, rewrite that row with the answer, the date, and Answered, then set `waiting_on` back (`references/recording-owner-answers.md`, sections 4 and 5).
   `toolkit work history <id> --note 'Owner said: <quote>' --effect '<what the answer changes>'`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Open Questions' --set-file <file>`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent`
6. A memory proposal: show its one line, and when it names a concept, the concept it would join. Recommend a yes only with evidence from this project (what he said, what happened, and when); with none, ask without a recommendation. Yes: approve it (a proposal for a concept is then added to it as a section). A proposal that names no concept: name the concept it goes in with `--concept`, an existing one of its type or a new key named for its subject, never for the fact (`references/proposals.md`, "Recording the owner's answer"). No: reject it, and never propose the same fact again.
   `toolkit memory list --type <type>`
   `toolkit memory approve <key> --by <owner>`
   `toolkit memory approve <key> --by <owner> --concept <type>_<subject> --title '<Concept title>' --description '<one-line summary of the concept>'`
   `toolkit memory reject <key>`
7. A decision for the whole project: add the row inside the `publish-docs` save workspace, in the order in `references/decisions-log.md`.
   `toolkit decision add --decision '<decision>' --why '<why>' --by <owner>`
8. A "no" or a change: record it as the answer, move the item back (for example to refinement), and open the skill that redoes the work.
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 02-refinement`
9. Lead with "Not saved" if any write failed. Update the current focus when an answer changed an item's next step (`references/current-focus.md`). After each recorded answer, list the decisions again and name what still waits on him, memory proposals included, by name ("One decision still waits: the memory proposal about Ghost slugs."). A decision an earlier reply said you would take next is taken next. Empty queue: say so and offer `work-on` for unblocked items. End with the next decision's question or the exact words that continue.
   `toolkit work decisions`

## Gotchas

- Run each `toolkit` command alone: never joined by `&&`, `;`, or a pipe, and never from a script (in Codex that runs it inside the sandbox, where it fails). One-line values go in single quotes, never double quotes; an apostrophe inside them is `'\''` in Claude Code and ’ (U+2019) in Codex, or reword the text. Section text goes on standard input (`--set-file -`) in Claude Code, and in `--text '<text>'` or a `mktemp -d` file in Codex (`references/toolkit-commands.md`, "Text in a command").
- Every decision carries a recommendation, even when it is the only one in the queue. A bare question is not enough. The one exception is a memory proposal with no evidence from this project (step 6).
- Ask in the reply text, never through a question tool.
- The approve command marks the Open Questions rows that asked for it Answered and prints "Marked Q-xx Answered". Never edit those rows again by hand.
- `waiting_on`: `agent` when the agent continues, `none` when nothing waits, `owner` while another of his questions on that item is still open. The approve command sets `none` by itself.
- A memory proposal is not a fact until he approves it. Do not rely on it.
- An approval never covers merge, deployment, spending, or publishing.
- After a result approval, the item continues with `work-finish`. Open it when he wants it shipped now.
- GitHub Issues or Jira: `toolkit work` exits with code 3. Build the queue from the labels in `references/tracker-github.md` or `references/tracker-jira.md`, and remove the waiting-on-owner label after each approval or last answer.

## Example decision message

```markdown
WI-015 needs your choice of design.

- Option A: use the built-in report page. Ready in about a day; the layout is fixed.
- Option B: a custom page. About a week; any layout you want.

I recommend A, because every requirement is met without custom code.
After A: I plan the build. After B: I plan a longer build and ask you about the layout.

Do you approve Option A?
```

# Work requirements

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Interviews the owner and writes what the result must do, never how to build it; every answer lands in the work item. Track these steps with the host's plan tool (Claude Code: the task list; Codex: `update_plan`), not in the reply.

## Steps

1. Find the item as `work-on` does; none exists, create it with his words as the Starting request. Requirements already approved and no change asked: open the skill the item's "Continue with" names and stop.
   `toolkit work show <id>`
   `toolkit work new --title '<title>' --type <type> --stage 01-discovery`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Starting request' --text '<his exact words>'`
2. Move it to refinement once requirements are being written. Before the first question, read the item and what the project already knows (`references/interview.md`, section 2).
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 02-refinement`
   `toolkit memory find '<topic>'`
3. Restate the goal in one sentence ("So the goal is X?"). Write the Agreed goal after a yes, and always before asking for approval.
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Agreed goal' --text '<goal>'`
4. Ask one question at a time, most basic first, each with a recommended answer and a short reason (`references/interview.md`, sections 3 and 4).
5. Save each answer before the next question: `R-xx` blocks and the Acceptance list in the format in `references/requirement-format.md`; anything unanswered as an Open Questions row, with the item waiting on the owner while one of his is open.
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Active requirements' --set-file <file>`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Open Questions' --append-row '| <next Q-id> | <question> | R-02 | Open | owner |'`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on owner`
6. A change to an approved requirement: edit the `R-xx`, keep the old wording in its Decision record, set it back to Refining, move the item to refinement, and say what the change affects when the item is past stage 03 (`references/interview.md`, section 7). The earlier approval stays on the record, and the stage command says so: it covered the requirements as they were, so ask him to approve the changed ones (step 8) before anything is built on them.
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 02-refinement`
7. Spec check, before asking for approval and whenever the owner says "check the spec": brief the `requirements-analyst` and handle its findings (`references/spec-check.md`).
8. Ask for approval and record his yes with the requirements checklist in `references/approvals.md`, section 2. Then a `build` or `data-load` item goes to `solution-design`, unless he agreed to skip the design.
   `toolkit work approve <id> --requirements --by <owner>`
9. Lead with "Not saved" on a failed write. Validate, update the current focus when the next step changed (`references/current-focus.md`), and hand back to `work-on` unless the owner stops. End with the one question or the exact words that continue.

# Memory criteria

This file is the project-specific selection policy: what is worth keeping in lasting memory. The approval policy, including onboarding and trusted mode, is in the `memory-save` skill, which saves with `toolkit memory save`. When the owner corrects what is worth saving, save the correction as a `feedback` memory with `memory-save`, as a general rule, without copying the rejected memory. Those `feedback` memories override this page.

## Default test for lasting memory

Save a topic when it concerns this project, has a credible source, would matter in a future session, would be costly or unreliable to reconstruct, and has no better maintained owner. Prefer updating an existing topic: a new fact goes under a heading in the topic file for its concept, and a new file is only for a new concept. A short pointer to an authoritative record can qualify when future sessions would otherwise miss that record.

| Type and filename | Usually worth retaining | Route or reject instead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `user_<topic>.md` | Relevant role, responsibility, working preference, or communication need the owner stated | Personal judgments, irrelevant biography, private details |
| `feedback_<topic>.md` | Repeated or standing correction to how the agent should work; confirmed selection lesson | One-off irritation, a rejected fact restated as policy, an instruction already in `AGENTS.md` |
| `project_<topic>.md` | Durable project constraint, rationale, technical landmark, or proven costly fix | A decision for the whole project (`DECISIONS.md`), code summary, schema copy, active ticket status, accepted requirement or design body |
| `reference_<topic>.md` | Hard-to-rediscover route to a source, system, dashboard, or decision record, with why to open it | Entire outside page or a path already obvious in `PROJECT.md` or the project map |

## Working context is different

`CURRENT_FOCUS.md` holds what is happening now: active work item IDs, what waits on the owner with no work item, untracked to-dos, and where the next session starts. It can change often. Keep a work item's detailed tasks and status in that item. Do not turn every open task into lasting memory. Do not discard an unresolved owner to-do merely to shorten the file.

## Never save as lasting memory

- Secrets, credentials, sensitive personal data, transcripts, scratch reasoning, raw logs, dropped guesses, or unsupported claims.
- A fact the same change already places in the authoritative file, unless a small route to that file is genuinely needed.
- Live status, pending approval, unshipped requirements, procedure steps, code restatements, or a current-system explanation that the code/System Guide owns.

# WI-001: Build the plain tip and total command — solution design

**Requirements:** WI-001  
**Design status:** Approved

**Design approval:** Approved by Mike Rihm on 2026-09-28

## What this design solves

A person running [WI-001's agreed goal](WORK-ITEM.md#agreed-goal) can see the tip and total for a restaurant bill and, when requested, each person's share. This design covers one terminal command and its checks. It does not add another way to run the calculation.

## Requirements and design readiness

The approved requirements describe a complete result for this small command. They settle accepted values, tip and total rounding, split rounding, output, and rejection of invalid values. The independent requirements check found no remaining gap. The command's internal parsing rules and error wording are implementation details; neither changes the required results.

| Requirement | Status in work item | Design coverage | Remaining decision or gap |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| R-01 — Show tip and total | Finalized | Option A, end-to-end behavior, requirement coverage, and technical shape | None |
| R-02 — Divide the total between friends | Finalized | Option A, end-to-end behavior, requirement coverage, and technical shape | None |

## What exists today

The repository has project records but no application JavaScript, `package.json`, or `bin/tipcalc.js`. The work item also records that no application code has been built. There is no existing calculation or command behavior to reuse or replace.

## Constraints and assumptions

| Type | Constraint or assumption | Source and status | Effect on the design |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Constraint | Run the command as `node bin/tipcalc.js 50 --percent 20`. | [WI-001 starting request](WORK-ITEM.md#starting-request), approved 2026-09-28 | Create `bin/tipcalc.js` for direct execution by Node. |
| Constraint | Accept nonnegative bill amounts and tip percentages and a positive whole-number split count. | [WI-001 R-01 and R-02](WORK-ITEM.md#active-requirements), approved 2026-09-28 | Validate input before calculation. |
| Constraint | Round Tip and Total half up to cents, meaning an exact half cent rounds to the higher cent; round a divided share upward to cents. | [WI-001 R-01 and R-02](WORK-ITEM.md#active-requirements), approved 2026-09-28 | Use exact whole-number arithmetic throughout. |
| Assumption | Bill amount appears first, `--percent` is required, and `--split` is optional; standard unsigned decimal text is accepted for bill and percentage. | Proposed command syntax derived from the [WI-001 starting request](WORK-ITEM.md#starting-request) | Parse the shown command shape; reject missing, duplicate, unknown, or malformed arguments. This does not narrow any numeric range in the requirements. |

## Design options

### Option A — One Node command with exact decimal arithmetic

#### Approach

Create `bin/tipcalc.js` using Node's built-in `process` object and `BigInt`. Parse decimal input as digits and a count of digits after the decimal point, without converting it to a JavaScript floating point number, which can only approximate many decimal values. Calculate cents as whole numbers, then format them as dollar amounts with two decimal places. Add focused checks using Node's built-in test runner and process execution facilities. No package or outside service is needed.

#### End-to-end behavior

1. The person runs `node bin/tipcalc.js <bill> --percent <percentage>` and may add `--split <count>`, for example `node bin/tipcalc.js 50 --percent 20 --split 3`.
2. The command checks the argument names, counts, and decimal values before calculating. If any value is missing or invalid, it writes an error to standard error (the terminal's error channel), exits with a nonzero status (a process result that signals failure), and prints no calculation to standard output (the terminal's normal output channel).
3. The command calculates the exact percentage of the original bill, rounds Tip to cents half up, adds that rounded Tip to the original bill, and rounds Total to cents half up. It prints `Tip: $10.00  Total: $60.00` for the example without a split.
4. When `--split` is present, the command divides the rounded Total in cents by the whole-number count, rounds a remainder upward by one cent, and prints `Each person pays: $20.00` on the second line for a split of three.

- **Data and state:** Input decimals become a nonnegative `BigInt` coefficient and a nonnegative decimal scale. For example, `10.005` becomes coefficient `10005` and scale `3`. Let the bill be `B / 10^b` dollars and the percentage be `P / 10^p`. Tip in cents before rounding is `B × P / 10^(b+p)`. For any nonnegative numerator `n` and positive denominator `d`, half-up rounding is `(2n + d) / (2d)` using whole-number division, which discards any fractional remainder. Apply it to Tip cents. Round bill cents from `B × 100 / 10^b` by the same rule, then add rounded Tip cents to get rounded Total cents. Because the rounded Tip is already a whole cent, this equals rounding the original bill plus the rounded Tip. For a split count `s`, each share in cents is `(totalCents + s - 1) / s` using whole-number division. No data persists.

# Interviewing the owner

How to run the requirements interview: what to read first, how to ask, how
to handle "grill me", resuming, and corrections. Everything the owner says
lands in the work item, never in a separate notes file.

## Contents

1. Aim at the outcome he wants
2. Before the first question
3. Asking
4. "Grill me" and "ask me questions"
5. Saving as you go
6. Resuming an interview
7. Corrections and changes
8. An example exchange

## 1. Aim at the outcome he wants

- Work toward the outcome the owner wants, not only the words he used. Read a
  rough answer in the context of that requirement's purpose and the rest of
  the system, and ask focused follow-up questions until the real intent is
  clear.
- Say so when an answer would undermine his own goal, conflict with a stated
  constraint, cause a problem elsewhere, or when a clearly better approach
  exists. Name the concern, the tradeoff, and the direction you recommend,
  then let him choose. Once he has heard the concern and decided, do it his
  way.
- Never quietly replace what he said with what you inferred.
- Keep it light. Do not read every answer back for approval, do not challenge
  every answer, and do not start designing while the goal is still open.

## 2. Before the first question

Read, so no question repeats an answer:

- the item: Starting request, Agreed goal, every `R-xx`, Open Questions, and
  Notes > Resume here;
- the area's file in `requirements/`, and `requirements/SYSTEM-DATA-MODEL.md`
  when data is involved;
- the area's file in `system-guide/`;
- project memory on the topic: `toolkit memory find '<topic>'`.

Ask only what the records and the code cannot answer.

## 3. Asking

- One question at a time, in the reply text, never through a question tool.
- Each question carries a recommended answer and a one-line reason, so the
  owner can confirm, correct, or redirect it.
- Settle upstream decisions before the ones that depend on them. Most basic
  first: who uses it, what they must be able to do, then the rules, then the
  exceptions.
- Follow contradictions and vague words ("fast", "easy", "secure") until
  they are resolved or recorded as open questions.
- The owner does not know: add an Open Questions row with who can answer, and
  go on with questions that do not depend on it. Offer a `researcher` when
  the fact can be found.
- He thinks out loud: let him. Save the settled parts as they come.
- Brainstorming methods from other plugins may run inside this skill. The
  answers still land in the work item.

## 4. "Grill me" and "ask me questions"

- "Grill me" means a deep interview: keep asking, one question at a time,
  until every branch that could change the result is covered.
- "Ask me questions first" means the interview comes before any build. It is
  not a batch of questions in one message.
- Near the end of every interview, ask: "What have we not touched that could
  change this?"

## 5. Saving as you go

Save each settled answer into the item before asking the next question. A
long interview fills the conversation; the item is the record that survives
a cleared context.

| He settles | Save it as |
| --- | --- |
| The goal ("So the goal is X?" and a yes) | The Agreed goal |
| A behavior, rule, or exception | An `R-xx` block (Status Refining) and, when it changes acceptance, the Acceptance list (`requirement-format.md`) |
| Something he cannot answer yet | An Open Questions row with who must answer; the item waits on him while one of his is open |
| An idea about how to build it | Notes > Solution options and considerations, linked to the `R-xx` |
| A lasting preference or lesson | A memory, through `memory-save` |

## 6. Resuming an interview

Read the item first. Continue from its Open Questions and Notes > Resume
here. Never start the interview again from the top.

## 7. Corrections and changes

- A correction to a requirement that is not yet approved needs no separate
  confirmation: apply it. Check the requirements and design it affects; ask
  only about consequences whose meaning is unclear.
- For a simple correction, say it in one sentence and ask only the next
  question that matters. Do not replay the whole item.
- A change to an approved requirement moves the item back to refinement and
  needs approval again. Keep the old wording in its Decision record.
- After stage 03, say what the change affects: the design, tasks already
  built, sub-items.
- Revisit Notes > Solution options and considerations when a requirement
  changes, so an old idea cannot quietly steer the design.

## 8. An example exchange

> Owner: Add a CSV export to the monthly report.
>
> Agent: So the goal is: anyone on the team can download the monthly report
> as a CSV file that opens in Excel? My recommendation is yes, with every
> column the report shows.
>
> Owner: Yes, but only managers.
>
> Agent (saves the Agreed goal, then R-01 "Managers can export the monthly
> report as CSV", Status Refining): Should archived rows be in the export? I
> recommend leaving them out, because the report hides them too.

The agent saved the goal and the first requirement before asking the second
question, and the second question carries a recommendation and a reason.

# Running `toolkit` commands

Purpose: how to run a `toolkit` command in Claude Code and in Codex, how to
pass text in one, and what each exit code means. Every skill that runs a
`toolkit` command follows this file.

## Contents

- Running toolkit commands
- Text in a command
- Exit codes
- Reporting a save
- Reading output and updating what you read
- Right and wrong examples

## Running toolkit commands

- Put each `toolkit` command on its own line and run it as a plain command,
  in both hosts. Do not join it to another command with `&&`, `;`, or a pipe,
  and do not wrap it in `$(...)`, a loop, or a script. This holds for read
  commands too: `toolkit work decisions && toolkit work show WI-001` is two
  commands, run one after the other.
- Why, in Codex: the project's command rule (`.codex/rules/toolkit.rules`)
  runs a `toolkit` command outside the sandbox only when it is the whole
  command. A `toolkit` command joined to anything else (`&&`, `;`, a pipe, a
  heredoc, `cd ... &&`) or run from a script (for example Python's
  `subprocess`) runs inside the Codex sandbox. The sandbox blocks Notion, the
  local Hindsight server, and the main checkout's `.work-items/` and
  `.memory/` from a worktree, so the command fails or reports the wrong
  cause.
- The one thing a Claude Code command may carry is its own text on standard
  input (`--set-file -` with a quoted heredoc; "Text in a command", below).
- Five commands ask the owner first, in both hosts, because they are hard or
  impossible to undo: `toolkit machine-setup`, `toolkit memory delete`,
  `toolkit memory import`, `toolkit import`, and
  `toolkit hindsight service install` or `start`. Get his yes in the reply
  before you run one. The host then asks him to confirm the command (Claude
  Code: a permission prompt; Codex: an approval). That prompt is expected, not
  an error.
- When the host refuses one of the five without asking him (Codex with
  approvals off: "approval required by policy, but AskForApproval is set to
  Never"), say that the cause is that approval setting, show him the exact
  command to run himself in a terminal, and wait. Do nothing in its place
  that he did not ask for: a refused delete is not a retire.
- In Codex, run each of those five alone, with `sandbox_permissions` set to
  `require_escalated` and a one-line reason. The approval alone keeps the
  command inside the sandbox, where it fails: `toolkit memory delete` cannot
  reach Hindsight or Notion, `toolkit machine-setup` cannot write `~/.codex`
  or `~/.local/bin`, `toolkit hindsight service install` cannot write
  `~/Library/LaunchAgents`, and `toolkit import` from a worktree cannot write
  the main checkout.
- Write `--json` and `--host` after the command words
  (`toolkit memory delete <key> --owner-approved --json`). The toolkit refuses
  those five commands when a flag comes first, because the ask-first rules
  would not match them.
- Never change a work item or a memory record with a script or a shell write
  (Python, Node, `sed -i`, `cat >`, `tee`, `cp`). Use the `toolkit` command
  that owns it. The hooks refuse the shell write, so it only wastes a step.
- `toolkit help <command>` prints every option of one command.

## Text in a command

The shell changes text before the command sees it. Inside double quotes it
runs anything between backticks and anything in `$(...)` as a command, and
puts that command's output in the text. The command then saves the text with
those parts missing and still reports success. So:

- **One-line values** (`--note`, `--effect`, `--append-row`, `--title`,
  `--reason`, `--quote`, `--evidence`, `--description`, `--source`): put them
  in single quotes, in both hosts. Inside single quotes the shell changes
  nothing. Never use double quotes for text.
- **An apostrophe inside single quotes:**
  - Claude Code: write it as `'\''`, for example
    `--note 'Owner said: "it'\''s ready, ship it"'`.
  - Codex: write it as ’ (the curly apostrophe, U+2019), or reword the text.
    Never `'\''` in Codex: the command rule does not match that form, so the
    command runs inside the sandbox, and the tool call can drop the
    backslash, which leaves a quote that is never closed.
- **Section, design, focus, glossary, and memory text in Claude Code:** pass
  it on standard input with `--set-file -` (or `--body-file -` for a memory
  save) and a quoted heredoc. The quotes around `EOF` in `<<'EOF'` stop the
  shell from changing anything in the text, and no file is left anywhere.
  Claude Code refuses `rm` outside the project, so a temporary file there
  could never be deleted. Write the command, then the text, then a line
  holding only `EOF`:

  ```text
  toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Overview' --set-file - <<'EOF'
  <the whole section text>
  EOF
  ```

- **The same text in Codex:** a heredoc runs the command inside the sandbox,
  so do not use one. Give short or medium text in single quotes
  (`--text '<text>'`; newlines inside the quotes are kept). For longer text:
  1. Make a new folder for this one save with `mktemp -d`. Its name is
     unique, so two sessions or two projects never share a file.
  2. Write the file in it with the file edit tool (`apply_patch`).
  3. Run the `toolkit` command alone, with the file's full path.
  4. Delete the file and the folder right after the command succeeds
     (`rm <file>`, then `rmdir <folder>`), before you ask the owner anything.

  Never write the file and run the `toolkit` command in one shell command.

  ```text
  toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Overview' --text '<text>'
  toolkit work design <id> --text '<text>' --status proposed
  toolkit memory focus --text '<text>' --expect <version>
  ```

- Never use a fixed file name such as `/tmp/wi001-requirements.md`. Every
  project starts at `WI-001`, so another session's save could land in this
  item.
- Never leave a draft file inside `.work-items/` or `.memory/`. A second
  `DESIGN.md`-shaped file there confuses the design lookup, and a stray note
  in `.memory/` is read as a memory.

## Exit codes

`toolkit help work` prints them as: "0 ok, 1 error, 2 validation failure or a
refused gate, 3 not supported for this tracker, 4 not a toolkit project."
`toolkit help memory` uses the same numbers: "1 error or not found, 2 refused
(a rule or a stale --expect), 3 not supported by this backend".

| Code | Meaning | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `0` | Done. | Read back what you wrote before you report it as saved ("Reporting a save", below). A "Note:" line in the output still needs action: report it to the owner, or do what it says. |
| `1` | Error, or the record was not found. | Read the message. It names the cause and usually the fix. Do not run the same command again unchanged. |
| `2` | Validation failure, a refused gate, or a stale `--expect`. | Fix what the message names and run the command again. A refused gate means an approval is missing: ask the owner for it. Never work around a refusal. |
| `3` | Not supported for this tracker or memory backend. | For a GitHub or Jira tracker, the message prints the path of the written instructions for that tracker. Follow them to make the same change on the issue. |
| `4` | Not a Toolkit V2 project. | Skip every work item and memory step and say so in one line. To set the project up, open the `project-setup` skill. |

`toolkit: command not found` means this computer cannot reach the command.
The `project-setup` skill fixes that.

## Reporting a save

- Save each settled answer before moving on, then read it back. A command
  that exits `0` is not proof by itself.
- A write failed: lead the reply with "Not saved". Name what was not saved
  and where it should go, and keep the text so it can be saved later.
- "Saved but not verified" in the output means the write happened and the
  read-back failed. The message names the first part that differs. Lead the
  reply with "Saved but not verified", say which part, and read the record
  back to judge it.

## Reading output and updating what you read

- Add `--json` when you need to read the output field by field, for example
  a record's `version`.
- `--expect <version>` tells the command which version of a record you read.
  The command refuses the save (exit `2`) when the record changed since then,
  so you never overwrite a newer edit. Read it again, merge, and save with the
  new version. `toolkit memory focus`, `toolkit memory glossary`, and
  `toolkit memory save` take it. `--expect absent` says it must not exist
  yet: a new record, or a project with no focus yet.

## Right and wrong examples

1. Two reads.
   - Wrong: `toolkit work list && toolkit work show WI-004`
   - Right: `toolkit work list`, then, as a second command,
     `toolkit work show WI-004`.
2. A history note that quotes the owner, with an apostrophe in his words.
   - Wrong: ``toolkit work history WI-004 --note "Owner said: it's ready, `ship it`"``
     (double quotes: the shell runs the words between the backticks as a
     command and saves its output in their place).
   - Right in Claude Code:
     `toolkit work history WI-004 --note 'Owner said: "it'\''s ready, ship it"'`
   - Right in Codex:
     `toolkit work history WI-004 --note 'Owner said: "it’s ready, ship it"'`
   - The prefix is `Owner said:`, which has no apostrophe to escape.
3. Section text in Codex.
   - Wrong: `cat > /tmp/overview.md <<'EOF' ... EOF && toolkit work edit WI-004 --section 'Overview' --set-file /tmp/overview.md`
     (one shell command, a heredoc, and a fixed file name).
   - Right: `toolkit work edit WI-004 --section 'Overview' --text '<text>'`
4. A change to a work item's header.
   - Wrong: `sed -i '' 's/^stage: .*/stage: 04-solution-design/' .work-items/WI-004/WORK-ITEM.md`
   - Right: `toolkit work set WI-004 --stage 04-solution-design --note '<why>'`
5. Toolkit commands from a script.
   - Wrong: `for id in WI-001 WI-002; do toolkit work show $id; done`
   - Right: `toolkit work show WI-001`, then `toolkit work show WI-002`, each
     as its own command.

# Work item and design format

What a work item and its design hold, their exact section names, and how to
change them with `toolkit work` commands without losing text.

## Contents

1. Where the record and the design live
2. Header fields
3. Sections of `WORK-ITEM.md`
4. Sections of `DESIGN.md`
5. Finding an item's file
6. Changing one section
7. Adding a table row
8. Editing a record directly
9. Titles
10. Generated files
11. Examples

## 1. Where the record and the design live

Every tracker uses the same body and the same design shape. Only the place
differs.

| Tracker | Work item | Design |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Local | `WORK-ITEM.md` in the item's folder under `.work-items/` | `DESIGN.md` beside it |
| Notion | The item's page in the project's Work Items database | The item's "Solution Design" child page |
| GitHub Issues | The issue body | One issue comment whose first line is `## Solution design` |
| Jira | The issue description | One comment whose first line is "Solution design" |

An item has one design home. Never make a separate design folder or a second
design file.

## 2. Header fields

The header (frontmatter locally, properties in Notion) holds these fields.
Only `toolkit work` commands change them.

| Field | Values | Changed by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | `WI-001` (the project's prefix and a number) | `toolkit work new`; never reused |
| `title` | The owner's words for the request | `toolkit work set <id> --title` |
| `type` | `discovery`, `solution-design`, `build`, `data-load`, `repository-maintenance`, `research`, `task`, `bug`, `enhancement`, or another lower-case word | `toolkit work set <id> --type` |
| `stage` | `01-discovery` to `14-spec-update` | `toolkit work set <id> --stage`, `approve`, `finish`, `cancel` |
| `status` | Backlog, Ready, In Progress, In Review, Done, Cancelled | Follows the stage; Done and Cancelled only through `finish` and `cancel` |
| `parent` | An item id or `none` | `toolkit work new --parent`, `toolkit work move` |
| `waiting_on` | `owner`, `agent`, `external: <who>`, `none` | `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on` |
| `priority` | `urgent`, `high`, `medium`, `low` | `toolkit work set <id> --priority` |
| `delivery` | `agent-led`, `owner-led`, `not-offered` | `toolkit work set <id> --delivery` |
| `requirements_approved` | `YYYY-MM-DD by <name>` or `no` | `toolkit work approve <id> --requirements` |
| `design` | `proposed`, `approved`, `superseded`, `none` | `toolkit work design`, `toolkit work approve <id> --design` |
| `result_approved` | `YYYY-MM-DD by <name>` or `no` | `toolkit work approve <id> --result`, `toolkit work finish --quote` |
| `updated` | `YYYY-MM-DD` | Every `toolkit work` write |

`toolkit work lifecycle` prints the stage labels, the statuses, and the types.
Blocked is not a status: an item that cannot move has `waiting_on` set and its
Overview Blockers line filled.

## 3. Sections of `WORK-ITEM.md`

These are the headings `--section` takes. A `###` subsection can be named on
its own, for example `--section 'Agreed goal'`.

| Heading | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `Overview` | Goal, Current position, Next action (and who owns it), Blockers, Related items (ids, never paths) |
| `Roadmap` | The phase table: Phase (`P1 — <name>`), Outcome, Status, Exit result, Sub-items |
| `Tasks` | One `### P1 — <name>` heading per phase, with checkbox tasks `P1-T01` (Work, Deliverable, Done when, Depends on) |
| `Recent History` | Dated rows: Date, Change or decision, Effect on the work (newest first) |
| `Open Questions` | Rows: ID (`Q-01`), Question, Affects, Status, Decision needed from (`owner` for the owner) |
| `Requirements` | Overall status and Finalization rule, then the subsections below |
| `Starting request` | The owner's own words for the request |
| `Agreed goal` | The outcome the owner agreed the item delivers |
| `Active requirements` | One `#### R-01 — <name>` block per requirement |
| `Acceptance` | The numbered list of what makes the whole item acceptable |
| `Notes` | The subsections below |
| `Decisions and context` | Context the next session needs that is not a requirement |
| `Resume here` | Where the next session picks up |
| `Solution options and considerations` | Build ideas, linked to an `R-xx`; never requirements |

The `R-xx` block fields are Status (Refining, Finalized, Superseded), Applies
to, Required behavior, Boundaries and exceptions, Acceptance check, Decision
record, and Open questions. Each field starts its own line.

In the local and Notion trackers, the requirements approval command sets the
Requirements "Overall status" line: never write that line by hand there.
GitHub Issues and Jira have no approve command, so after the owner's yes the
agent writes Finalized there itself (`tracker-github.md` or `tracker-jira.md`,
"The `toolkit work` steps").

## 4. Sections of `DESIGN.md`

The CLI writes the design's header fields: `work_item`, `status` (`proposed`,
`approved`, `superseded`), and `approved`.

| Heading | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| Header lines | Requirements (the item id), Design status, Requirements checked, Last updated, Design approval |
| `What this design solves` | Who uses the result, what they need, what must be true afterward, and what is left to another item |
| `Requirements and design readiness` | One row per `R-xx`: its status in the item, the design coverage, the remaining decision or gap |
| `What exists today` | Verified current behavior and files, or "nothing exists yet" |
| `Constraints and assumptions` | One row each, with source, status, and effect on the design |
| `Design options` | `### Option A — <name>` (then B, C), each with Approach, End-to-end behavior, Requirement coverage, Technical shape, Tradeoffs and risks, Build order |
| `Option comparison` | Only with more than one option |
| `Recommendation and owner decision` | Recommendation, Owner decision, Reason for decision |
| `Selected design` | After the owner chooses: End-to-end flow; Components and responsibilities; Data, access, and integration details; Edge cases and failure behavior; Release and ongoing operation |
| `Diagrams` | Mermaid diagrams, each with a heading and a one-sentence explanation |
| `Build and verification plan` | Technical sequence, and Acceptance checks (one row per requirement) |
| `Sources and decisions that affect the build` | Claim or decision, source, date, evidence type, how it was checked |
| `Where a builder could misread this design` | Requirement or section, plausible wrong reading, intended reading |
| `Notes` | Open design questions, Design changes during the interview, Current position and next step |

Keep every heading exactly as the template has it, including the dash in
`Option A — <name>`. In the local and Notion trackers, never write "Approved"
in the Design status line: a save replaces that line with the stored status,
and only `toolkit work approve <id> --design --by <owner>` approves a design.
GitHub Issues and Jira have no approve command, so after the owner's yes the
agent writes Approved there itself (`tracker-github.md` or `tracker-jira.md`).

## 5. Finding an item's file

Never build a path by hand. The owner may have moved or renamed the folder.

```text
toolkit work show <id> --path
```

`toolkit work show <id>` also prints the item's stage, who it waits on, the
skill that continues it, its parent and sub-items, its design (or the
parent's approved design it inherits), and the worktree branch and folder to
use.

## 6. Changing one section

1. Read the section. The output is the whole section as it stands.
   `toolkit work show <id> --section '<heading>'`
2. Change only what needs to change. Keep the rest word for word.
3. Leave out the section's fill-in guide comment (`<!-- ... -->`) once the
   section holds real content.
4. Write the whole section back. `<file>` is `-` in Claude Code, with the text
   on standard input; in Codex use `--text '<text>'` or a file in a new
   `mktemp -d` folder (`toolkit-commands.md`, "Text in a command").
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section '<heading>' --set-file <file>`
5. Read it back. An exit code of `0` is not proof by itself.
   `toolkit work show <id> --section '<heading>'`

To remove the template's fill-in guide above Overview:

```text
toolkit work edit <id> --remove-guide
```

## 7. Adding a table row

Add one row to Open Questions or Recent History with `--append-row` and the
full Markdown row in single quotes.

A new question takes the next free `Q-` number: read the Open Questions
section first and add one to the highest number there (`Q-01` when there is
none). "Decision needed from" is `owner` for the owner, or a person or role.
When you asked it with a recommendation, the Question cell holds both:
the question, then "Recommended: <answer>, because <reason>."

```text
toolkit work show <id> --section 'Open Questions'
toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Open Questions' --append-row '| Q-03 | Should the export include archived rows? | R-02 | Open | owner |'
```

A history row is added with its own command, which writes the date:

```text
toolkit work history <id> --note '<what happened>' --effect '<what it changes>'
```

To answer a question, rewrite its row in the whole Open Questions section:
the answer, the date, and status Answered. An approve command or a
`--delivery` answer marks the rows that asked for it Answered by itself and
prints "Marked Q-xx Answered"; do not edit those rows again.

## 8. Editing a record directly

- Prefer `toolkit work edit`. It works in every tracker the CLI drives and
  keeps the CLI's record of what it wrote.
- A local record's body text may also be changed with the file edit tool. The
  post-tool hook checks the record after the edit.
- Never change the header fields with a file edit, and never create a record
  with one. The pre-tool hook refuses both, because they would skip the
  approval gates.
- Never write a record from the shell: no `cat >`, `tee`, `sed -i`, `cp`, and
  no Python or Node script. The hook refuses it, so it only wastes a step.
- A Notion item changes only through `toolkit work` commands. Never write its
  page with another Notion tool.

## 9. Titles

- A new item's title uses the owner's own words for the request. When you
  shorten them, say the title in one line in the reply ("I started WI-003,
  'Write a short project brief'.").
- To retitle an item, say the new title to the owner in one line first. Never
  retitle quietly.
  `toolkit work set <id> --title '<new title>'`

## 10. Generated files

Never edit these by hand or from the shell. The hooks refuse it.

- `.work-items/DASHBOARD.md`: rebuilt by every `toolkit work` write and by
  `toolkit work sync`.
- `.work-items/.toolkit-state.json`: the id-to-path map and the highest id
  used.

## 11. Examples
